Why does a tmux session name containing a dot break every bare -t target?
Why does a tmux session name containing a dot break every bare -t target?

Short answer: a -t target is parsed as session:window.pane, so a dot inside the session name is read as the window/pane separator. The lookup then runs against a window or a pane that does not exist, and the error names that window or pane rather than the session — which is why it reads as a missing session. Keep dots out of session names.
Why does a tmux session name containing a dot break every bare -t target?
The parse, and where the name goes
Why does a tmux session name containing a dot break every bare -t target?
session:window.pane is the target form. Every part is optional, so hay-.F is not rejected as malformed — it is accepted and split, with F taken as the pane.
Why does a tmux session name containing a dot break every bare -t target?
The parse, and where the name goes

The split happens on the first : and the first ., wherever they sit. A dot at the start of a suffix, in the middle of one, or in the middle of the name all break the same way; only the reported half changes.

The message moves with the dot. hay-.F reports a missing pane; hay-D.F reports a missing window named hay-D, a string that appears nowhere. Two instances of one fault do not look alike, so recognising the second from having debugged the first does not happen.

A script's existence check returns 1, the same as for a session that is genuinely absent. Nothing downstream can tell a missing session from an unusable name, so the guard that would catch this is the thing the fault disables.

The workarounds, and why they are not a convention
Why does a tmux session name containing a dot break every bare -t target?
A trailing colon disambiguates — -t '=hay-.F:' exits 0 — and an explicit window works too: -t '=hay-.F:0' lists panes normally.
Why does a tmux session name containing a dot break every bare -t target?
The workarounds, and why they are not a convention

Both are correct and neither is safe to build on. A naming scheme that holds only while everyone remembers a trailing colon fails at the first bare target anyone writes, including one written by a tool. An explicit window is also the case that hides the fault during testing: it is the one target shape a stray dot leaves alone, so a probe built from session:0 targets passes on every input it is given.

Why does a tmux -t =session target fail in Zsh?
Why does a tmux -t =session target fail in Zsh?
Short answer: Zsh eats the = before tmux ever sees it. =word is zsh's equals expansion, which substitutes the full path of the command word — and errors when there is no such command. Quote it:
Why does a tmux -t =session target fail in Zsh?
Why does a tmux -t =session target fail in Zsh?

To tmux, a leading = on a -t target means exact match: -t =mysession matches the session named exactly mysession rather than the first session with that prefix. Useful whenever two sessions share a prefix — hayward-2026-08-24 and hayward-2026-08-24-scratch.
Why does a tmux -t =session target fail in Zsh?
To Zsh, a leading = on an unquoted word means look up this command and substitute its path. The two conventions collide on exactly the argument where the tmux one is wanted.
Why does a tmux -t =session target fail in Zsh?
Why does a tmux -t =session target fail in Zsh?
The failure is reported by zsh, before the command runs at all. Nothing named tmux appears in the message, which is what makes it read like a missing session rather than a shell expansion.
Why does a tmux -t =session target fail in Zsh?
It is an option, and it is on by default
Why does a tmux -t =session target fail in Zsh?
The behavior is the EQUALS option. setopt does not list it, because setopt prints only what differs from the default — so its absence from that listing is what tells you it is on.
Why does a tmux -t =session target fail in Zsh?
It is an option, and it is on by default
The negative test is what settles it:
Why does a tmux -t =session target fail in Zsh?
It is an option, and it is on by default
Turning EQUALS off globally is the wrong fix. Quoting is local, needs no shell state, and is correct in every shell.

Why does a tmux -t =session target fail in Zsh?

Any tmux command taking a target: new-window -t, split-window -t, send-keys -t, respawn-pane -t, has-session -t. Session, window, and pane targets are all affected, since the exact-match prefix is a property of the target syntax rather than of any one command.
Why does a tmux -t =session target fail in Zsh?

Bash has no equals expansion, so a script that worked when run with bash fails when the same line is pasted into an interactive zsh prompt — measured on 2026/08/24 against -t =reeve-2026-08-24, which failed with reeve-2026-08-24 not found.
Why does a tmux -t =session target fail in Zsh?
Why does a tmux -t =session target fail in Zsh?
zshexpn(1) — Filename Expansion — "If a word begins with an unquoted = … the rest of the word is taken as the name of a command … replaced with the full pathname."

tmux(1) man page — COMMANDS — a target beginning with = must match exactly.

Why doesn't prefix Alt-Left or Alt-Right resize the inner horizontal split in a nested tmux layout (outer top-bottom split and lower left-right split), while Alt-Up or Alt-Down still move the outer boundary?
Why doesn't prefix Alt-Left or Alt-Right resize the inner horizontal split in a nested tmux layout (outer top-bottom split and lower left-right split), while Al
Why doesn't prefix Alt-Left or Alt-Right resize the inner horizontal split in a nested tmux layout (outer top-bottom split and lower left-right split), while Al

Short answer: The tmux/Keyshort/Pane/Resize Pane bindings are still calling resize-pane on the active pane. In a nested layout they only move the immediate vertical border between the two bottom panes. If that border cannot move—most often because the other bottom pane is already at tmux’s minimum width—the command no-ops, which looks like “resize doesn’t work.” Alt-Up / Alt-Down still move the outer (full-width) horizontal divider, where there is usually more slack in rows than you have spare columns in the bottom row, so those resizes are more likely to succeed.
Why doesn't prefix Alt-Left or Alt-Right resize the inner horizontal split in a nested tmux layout (outer top-bottom split and lower left-right split), while Al
Why doesn't prefix Alt-Left or Alt-Right resize the inner horizontal split in a nested tmux layout (outer top-bottom split and lower left-right split), while Al

resize-pane -L / -R / -U / -D nudges the edge of the current pane in that direction against its sibling along that axis, inside the layout “cell” that already contains the pane (tmux(1) — resize-pane).

The maintainer describes this as resizing up to the limit of the cell that contains the active pane; resize-pane does not recursively shrink or grow panes outside that cell the way dragging borders with the mouse sometimes can in awkward layouts (tmux issue #1774, issue #4381).
Why the inner left/right split often “won’t budge”
Why doesn't prefix Alt-Left or Alt-Right resize the inner horizontal split in a nested tmux layout (outer top-bottom split and lower left-right split), while Al

Minimum pane size: tmux enforces a minimum width and height for panes (on the order of a few cells; see discussion around PANE_MINIMUM in tmux issue #1480). If bottom-left is already as narrow as allowed, you cannot steal more columns for bottom-right, so both horizontal nudges can appear dead until you first give slack (e.g. widen the left pane with the opposite horizontal resize, or resize from the other pane).
Why the inner left/right split often “won’t budge”

Asymmetric slack: After a top/bottom split, the bottom row may be short in height but still wide; the limiting factor for horizontal resize is columns shared with the sibling, not the whole window. Vertical resize of the outer split uses full window width and many rows, so it succeeds more often even in the same session.
Why the inner left/right split often “won’t budge”

Run tmux/list-keys (pipe through rg resize if you like) and confirm prefix + M-Left / M-Right are bound to resize-pane -L / -R as expected for oh-my-tmux.
Check pane widths with tmux display-message -p '#{pane_width}' after select-pane -L / -R to see whether the sibling is pinned at a tiny width (minimum-size panes block further horizontal steals).
If you need deeper layout changes than one border, use resize-pane -t <target> on specific panes, select-layout, or mouse dragging (Super User — adjusting split sizes).
